title: 4 Physician Scheduling Options for Private Practices
description: Physician scheduling for private practices and provider groups: managed services, spreadsheets, self-service software and EHR-native modules.
content:
Summary

  • Physician practices often spend 4-8 hours per month just building the initial draft of their schedules, a significant administrative drain.
  • There are four categories of scheduling tools, covering five named tools and services, each designed to solve a different problem, from patient booking to internal provider coordination.
  • Most tools focus on what happens after a schedule is made (viewing or filling it), not the complex task of creating a fair physician schedule from scratch.
  • If your core problem is the time and complexity of building fair call, rotation, and clinic schedules, a managed service like Scheduling Wizard is designed to solve it for you.

You built your practice around medicine, not spreadsheets. Yet somehow, a surprising chunk of your week gets swallowed by the scheduling puzzle: who's on call Thursday, who swapped last weekend, whether the fairness math still holds up across the quarter. According to physicians on forums like r/hospitalist, it takes anywhere from 4 to 8 hours a month just to produce the first draft of a schedule, and that's before the swaps, last-minute changes, and "can you just carry it in your head" fairness tracking that adds up all month long.

The problem isn't that no tools exist. The problem is that the market is flooded with solutions that solve different problems, and choosing the wrong category means paying for something that doesn't actually fix your pain.

This guide breaks down five private practice physician scheduling tools and services across four categories. For each, we cover the ideal use case, real limitations, and approximate cost tier, so you can make a strategic decision, not just pick the most-advertised product.

1. Managed Scheduling Services

Best for: Complex multi-provider practices that want to stop building schedules entirely.

This is the most differentiated category on this list and the one most practices overlook. A managed scheduling service isn't software you log into, it's a done-for-you service where you submit your rules, coverage requirements, physician preferences, and fairness rules, and receive a complete schedule as a finished output. No learning curve. No configuration. No more carrying the logic in your head.

Scheduling Wizard

Scheduling Wizard is our entry in this category, built for the complexity that defines physician scheduling. A YC-backed (W26) managed service, Scheduling Wizard is a team that builds schedules full time: complete Block, Clinic, Call, and Attending schedules. You submit your rules (vacation requests, elective preferences, coverage minimums, fairness parameters) and receive the finished schedule, delivered as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you, ready for whatever platform your practice already uses.

This matters because it directly addresses the single biggest pain in physician scheduling: not just the initial build, but, as one hospitalist put it, "swapping duties last minute and maintaining fairness over months... that's what really adds up." Scheduling Wizard takes the build and the fairness arithmetic off your team.

Why it's different from software: Tools like QGenda are powerful, but as physicians note, "getting QG to actually do what you want isn't easy, and learning how it works is very complicated." Scheduling Wizard removes that burden entirely. There is no software to master, no annual re-onboarding when your senior scheduler leaves, and no institutional knowledge lost between turnover cycles. We hold the fairness and coverage targets in the build, rather than leaving you to track them by hand.

Key capabilities include:

  • Call schedules with fair call distribution
  • Block/rotation and clinic schedule coordination
  • Resident and physician preference integration (vacation, electives, conferences)
  • Conflict detection and full coverage (no gaps, no overstaffing)
  • Redrafts around unplanned absences

Ideal use case: Private practices with 10+ providers, complex call structures, or multi-site scheduling needs where the administrative and cognitive burden of manual scheduling has become a real operational cost.

Key limitations: Less suited for practices that want to make constant real-time manual micro-adjustments themselves. This is a service model, not a self-serve dashboard.

Cost: quoted per group. Meaningful, and often justified when you calculate what physician or administrator time spent on scheduling actually costs.

2. Excel / Google Sheets

Best for: Practices whose coverage rules and partner arrangements change faster than any platform can be reconfigured.

Most practice schedules are still built in a spreadsheet, which is why it belongs second rather than last. It will take contract terms, site splits, partner preferences and the arrangements that were never written down, and it will take them the moment you think of them. Google Sheets lets the whole group work in one file and see what changed.

What it does not do is the counting. Call equity across a year, weekend and holiday balance, and coverage minimums at every site are arithmetic, and arithmetic done by hand between clinics is where disputes start. It also holds the schedule without holding the reasoning, so it does not transfer when the person who built it steps back.

3. Self-Service Scheduling Software

Best for: Solo practitioners and small single-specialty practices with straightforward booking needs.

Self-service scheduling software is the most accessible category: SaaS tools you buy, configure, and manage yourself. They're designed to help practices set up online appointment booking, automated reminders, and patient intake forms without requiring a large IT team.

Acuity Scheduling

Acuity Scheduling is one of the most popular tools in this tier. It allows practices to offer 24/7 online booking, send automated appointment reminders to reduce no-shows, and collect intake information before the visit. It's intuitive to set up and works well for straightforward, appointment-based scheduling flows.

Key limitations: Acuity has no native EHR integration and limited multi-provider support, which means it breaks down quickly as scheduling complexity increases. It works well for a solo dermatologist booking cosmetic consults; it's not the right fit for a hospitalist group managing call shifts, swaps, and fairness tracking across 20 physicians.

Healthie

Healthie is another self-service option popular among smaller practices, particularly in the behavioral health and wellness space. It includes scheduling alongside telehealth, billing, and charting in a lightweight package. Still, like most self-service tools, it's built around patient appointment booking, not the harder job of building a provider schedule.

Ideal use case: A solo or small-group practice with simple, repeatable appointment types and no complex call or rotation scheduling requirements.

Key limitations: Self-service tools are built for appointment flows, not for workforce rules. If your scheduling involves variable shift lengths (8h, 24h, full weeks), fairness balancing, or multi-site coordination, you'll outgrow these tools quickly.

4. EHR-Native Schedulers

Best for: Mid-to-large practices or hospital-affiliated groups already deeply embedded in an EHR ecosystem.

EHR-native scheduling modules are built directly into systems like Epic, Cerner, or Meditech, or designed as deeply integrated companions to them. The core value proposition is a single source of truth: patient data, appointments, clinical notes, and billing all live in one system, reducing the risk of data silos and manual data re-entry.

Luma Health

Luma Health is one of the strongest examples in this category. It offers bidirectional integration with 70+ EHR systems and uses AI to automate patient outreach, reminders, and scheduling, all flowing directly into the practice's existing clinical workflow. If your team already lives inside an EHR all day, Luma Health extends that environment rather than adding another platform to manage.

Key limitations: EHR-native schedulers are excellent at managing patient appointment flow, but they are not built to balance a provider schedule. Features like call fairness balancing, shift swap tracking, or complex rotation logic simply aren't in scope for most EHR scheduling modules. Customization typically requires expensive vendor involvement or internal IT resources, neither of which is quick or cheap.

Ideal use case: Practices where data integration and a unified patient record are the primary concern, and where provider schedule complexity is relatively low.

Approximate cost tier: High, often bundled within broader EHR licensing, which for full enterprise systems can run into the hundreds of thousands annually.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the main difference between Scheduling Wizard and software like QGenda or Amion?

Scheduling Wizard is a done-for-you service that builds your complex physician schedule for you, while tools like QGenda and Amion are for viewing and managing a schedule that has already been created. We build the finished schedule and deliver it as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. You then upload that finished schedule into your existing platform for your team's daily use. We replace the hours of manual work spent building the schedule, not the tool your team uses to see it.

What rules does a managed service build a practice schedule around?

Coverage minimums first, then call equity, contractual obligations, time off and requests, and multiple sites where the practice has them. During onboarding we collect all of it, including the rules nobody writes down, and build the schedule around them. A practice has no ACGME requirement; that applies to residency and fellowship programs, and we build those too.

What if our group is attached to a training program?

Then two sets of rules apply at once, and they interact. The residents and fellows carry the ACGME duty hour requirements, including at-home call activity counting toward the 80-hour weekly limit. The attendings carry the group's own coverage and supervision obligations. We build both schedules together so one does not break the other.

What happens when something changes mid-year, like a leave or a new site?

You tell us what changed and we rebuild the rest of the schedule to the same rules, with coverage and fairness intact. Redrafts through the year are part of the service.

Who is the ideal user for a managed scheduling service?

The ideal user is any medical group, private practice, or residency program that finds the process of building, balancing, and maintaining physician schedules to be a significant administrative burden. This service is best for groups with 10+ providers, complex call or rotation structures, multi-site coverage needs, or a training program attached to the group. If you're spending more than a few hours each month on scheduling spreadsheets, the model is likely to fit.

Why is Scheduling Wizard a service rather than self-serve software?

Scheduling Wizard is a service because building a fair physician schedule to every rule at once is specialized work, not a simple configuration task. Self-serve software often has a steep learning curve and still requires you to carry the complex scheduling logic in your head. By providing a "done-for-you" service, we remove the burden of learning new software and take the build off your plate, with fairness and coverage as part of it.

How are physician preferences and vacation requests handled?

All physician preferences, including vacation requests, conference dates, and specific call/shift preferences, are submitted as inputs before the schedule is built. Our team builds around them as far as the coverage rules allow, and tells you where a request could not be honored and why, so the trade-off is yours rather than a surprise.
